It's also an enthralling, emotional knockout and the first must-see play of the season.
Both times I've seen the play I've felt unprepared for the emotional wallop it lands, the way that Wohl's work becomes cosmically immense.

In Bess Wohl's galvanizing show of the hour "Liberation," directed by Whitney White, the women in a nineteen-seventies consciousness-raising group wrestle with questions political and personal while building solidarity and coalition.
She makes everyone care about the questions she has herself and that’s exactly what a playwright should be doing.
The miracle of this play is that the circle feels as if it is extending to embrace us all.
“Liberation” is a brilliant, well-acted, and sobering account of the women’s rights movement, complicity, and the lens through which we view our caretakers — namely, our mothers.
Liberation is a welcome original play on Broadway that relies not on marquee Hollywood names for buzz but a slate of strong performances.
Even if Wohl’s play is overlong and ambles repetitively at times, there’s nothing didactic or “eat your spinach” about the enjoyable and touching story of a weekly women’s group in 1970s Ohio.
So much of Liberation—Wohl's best play, and she's had some excellent ones, including Small Mouth Sounds and Make Believe—feels like a radical act.
I’ve found myself mentally comparing everything else onstage to Liberation, and frankly, not many other shows compare. Liberation is a must see.
It is a great American play, and you should do everything in your power to catch it before its final bow on February 1, 2026.
This is one of those rare productions in which each performer has become so entwined with the character that all future iterations will most assuredly be a pale imitation.
At a time when the idea of progress feels fragile, Wohl’s play insists that the search for freedom, whether personal or political, is never finished.
This fizzingly vibrant ideas’ play seeks and elicits that level of interaction from the audience—particularly the women watching.

Liberation may not be able to answer life's difficult questions, but it knows that it's important to foster these conversations and to come together to try our best to make the world a better place — especially when history often seems hellbent on repeating itself.

But thanks to this powerful, life-affirming play, we do know that for a while she found a sisterhood that supported her, and sustained her, and awakened her to the possibility of real change in the world and in herself.
On Broadway, it’s a revelation of the highest order, possibly the best of the season.
Exquisitely acted by an eight-person ensemble and directed with extraordinary acuity by Whitney White, “Liberation” proves to be must-see theater.

Liberation is a potent exercise in time travel to the era of Betty Friedan and Ms. Magazine, George McGovern and Richard Nixon (the latter included in a showstopping revelation), all presented without a whiff of nostalgia or condescension.
Sharply imagined, heartbreaking in places, and unexpectedly funny throughout, Liberation lays bare the contradictions of a movement that fell short in many ways, but is still urgently needed today.

A bold, thought-provoking show that dives into misogyny, gender roles and domestic abuse, while exploring friendship, legacy and what it really means to be free, all with humor and honesty seamlessly woven throughout.

They may enter as archetypes, but they emerge as women in motion — messy, funny, flawed, and searching. Betsy Aidem’s Margie is a housewife fraying at the seams as her retired husband clogs her oxygen. Audrey Corsa’s Dora is a young corporate climber outpacing a sea of male mediocrity.
Liberation balances both intellect and heart, which makes for a remarkable night of theater.
I wish the show were less relevant, but because of how necessary this production is, I simply cannot pick it apart like a stagnant work of art.
Wohl’s play remains an important document of an earlier time when women’s liberation seemed just around the corner.
This play will not shake the building or linger in your mind for long.
